platforms.name: Claude Enterprise (Anthropic) — live changelog, two new entries
details: **Compliance API returns local session transcripts (Aug 11, beta, Claude Enterprise only).** Three endpoints — `GET /v1/compliance/apps/sessions/local` (list, `clls_` IDs), `GET /v1/compliance/apps/sessions/local/{session_id}` (metadata), `GET /v1/compliance/apps/sessions/local/{session_id}/messages` (transcript). Uses the **existing Compliance Access Key and `read:compliance_user_data` scope — no new key, scope, setting or client update**. Admin API keys are rejected with 403. `product_surface` is `cowork` (Claude Desktop) or `claude_code` (terminal, Desktop, or IDE extension). Transcripts contain user prompts, assistant text, `tool_use` and `tool_result` blocks, with **MCP tool calls and most server tool calls normalized into those same shapes**; `CLAUDE.md` appears as ordinary user content and skill content appears when the client sends it. Excluded: thinking blocks, the system prompt (a synthetic marker stands in), **tool definitions and MCP server configuration**, and all binary blocks. Retention 6 years or the org's custom conversation retention period. Read-only — no deletion through the API. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/compliance-sessions#retrieve-local-sessions

**`anthropic-workspace-id` response header (Aug 11).** Every Claude API response now carries the `wrkspc_`-prefixed ID of the workspace that the request's API key or access token resolved to, including the organization's Default Workspace. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/workspaces
*(Not reported: Aug 10 Claude Sonnet 5 pricing decision — pricing.)*

platforms.name: Microsoft Foundry — roll-up unfroze; five new agent-platform surfaces
details: **Enable incoming A2A on a Foundry agent (preview)** — ms.date 2026-08-12, updated 2026-08-13, the freshest item in this scan. Exposes an agent **as** an A2A server; this monitor had previously only covered the outgoing direction. Enabled by a single PATCH setting `agent_card` plus `agent_endpoint.protocol_configuration.a2a`; **not available in the Foundry portal**, REST/SDK only. Serves **both A2A v1.0 and v0.3 on the same base path**, with version chosen by agent-card discovery, the `A2A-Version` header, or `?a2a-version=` — and **v0.3 is served by default when unspecified**. Cards are published at `…/protocols/a2a/agentCard/v1.0` and `…/agentCard/v0.3`, carrying description, version and a **`skills[]`** array. All A2A URLs require Entra ID auth (**anonymous agent-card access is not supported**) and the caller needs **Foundry Agent Consumer** or higher. Callers authenticate either **on-behalf-of the end user** or with a **service identity**. v1.0 is JSONRPC-only; text modality only; no streaming. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/enable-agent-to-agent-endpoint

**Managed MCP servers powered by connector namespaces (preview)** — ms.date 2026-07-28. The Foundry Tools Catalog carries **over 1,000 connectors**; adding one makes Foundry provision a **managed MCP server**. Every Foundry account has a **Connector Namespace** hosting connector runtimes and MCP servers, with **each project mapped to an environment** in it. Only selected connector *actions* become tools; triggers are unsupported. Auth is **OAuth2 with a one-time per-end-user consent** minted via `listConsentLinks`. The project connection is `authType: OAuth2`, `category: RemoteTool`, `metadata.type = gateway_connector`; `target` begins as the literal `https://placeholder` and is rewritten to a **`logic.azure.com/api/connectorGateways/…/mcp` gateway URL**. Four publisher tiers with explicitly different data responsibility, down to **independent publishers at a "lower certification bar"**. Critically: **only validated connectors are gated in the portal — the REST/SDK/`azd` path has no gating at all.** Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/tools/connectors

**Restrict access to sensitive content in Foundry traces (preview)** — ms.date 2026-07-21. Seven OpenTelemetry gen-AI attributes are classed as sensitive — `gen_ai.input.messages`, `gen_ai.output.messages`, `gen_ai.system_instructions`, **`gen_ai.tool.definitions`**, **`gen_ai.tool.call.arguments`**, **`gen_ai.tool.call.result`**, `gen_ai.evaluation.explanation` — and routed to a dedicated **`AppGenAIContent`** Log Analytics table that can be set Protected, readable only by the **Privileged Monitoring Data Reader** role. **From September 30, 2026 these values stop being written to `AppDependencies`/`AppTraces`/`AppEvents`**, leaving only a pointer. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/observability/how-to/traces-sensitive-content

**Microsoft Foundry Canvas (preview)** — ms.date 2026-07-21. A **GitHub Copilot App extension** (Settings > Plugins > `microsoft-foundry`) that designs, configures, tests and deploys Foundry **hosted agents** from an editor side panel. Signs in to Azure, enumerates subscriptions and projects, browses the project's deployed models, **toolboxes, tools, skills and guardrails**, runs the agent locally in an embedded **Agent Inspector**, and publishes with **Deploy to Foundry** — both backed by `azd` commands. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/foundry-canvas

**Microsoft Foundry Notification Center** — ms.date 2026-07-09. In-portal aggregated alert feed spanning **Microsoft Defender for Cloud security alerts** (malicious activity, content-safety violations), **Azure Policy and Foundry guardrail compliance violations**, and run completion/failure events. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/concept-notification-center

*(Not reported: `azure.yaml` authoring, WebSocket mode for the Responses API, Foundry IQ private agentic retrieval tutorials, Claude model hosting comparison, hosted-agent OpenTelemetry export, toolbox authentication — extensions of surfaces already covered. The Foundry blog's newest posts, both Aug 12, cover Azure Content Understanding, a content-extraction service rather than an agent surface.)*

platforms.name: ChatGPT Enterprise (OpenAI) — three new capabilities in four days
details: **Computer History (Aug 13, opt-in, macOS desktop).** Turns activity across apps and websites into **memories and a timeline** that ChatGPT and Codex can use. Records interaction events exposed through **macOS accessibility features** — clicks, typing, keyboard shortcuts, app switching. It **replaces the Chronicle research preview** and is a rebuild rather than a rename: Chronicle used screenshots, Computer History does not capture screenshots, screen recordings, microphone input or system audio. Mechanism: events are captured locally, then Computer History **periodically starts an ephemeral Codex session with access to the interaction-event stream** to summarize activity into memories; temporary event files are processed on OpenAI servers and not retained after processing or used for training, and the resulting **plain-text memory files are stored locally on the Mac**. Events are held on-device for up to 48 hours. Off by default; Pro users can self-enable, but **Business and Enterprise require an administrator to grant access first**. Users control which apps and websites contribute and can pause collection from the menu bar. Not available in the EEA, Switzerland or the UK. Source: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/customization/computer-history

**Import from another agent (Aug 11).** The ChatGPT desktop app imports **instructions, settings, skills, plugins, projects and recent work** from **Claude Code, Claude Cowork and Cursor**, via Settings > Import, with an option for **automatic updates that keep imported work in sync with the original agent**. Codex CLI has the same flow via `/import` for Claude Code and Cursor, covering setup, project files and recent chats. Source: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/import

**Daybreak Blue and Daybreak Red tiers (Aug 10).** Two new access tiers in OpenAI's Daybreak "Trusted Access for Cyber" program. **Blue** covers approved defensive workflows — secure code review, vulnerability triage, detection engineering, incident response, malware analysis, patch validation — on GPT-5.6 Sol. **Red** adds advanced defensive *and offensive* work with access to purpose-trained **GPT-5.5-Cyber and GPT-5.6-Cyber**: vulnerability research, exploit validation, security testing. OpenAI's published internal evaluation: **GPT-5.6-Cyber handled 95% of advanced cybersecurity prompts** covering exploit-chain development, authentication bypass and privilege escalation, **versus 1.5% for GPT-5.6 Sol with default protections**. Source: https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001258-openai-daybreak-trusted-access-for-cyber-overview
**Linux desktop app preview (Aug 11)** — Ubuntu, Debian and Fedora, x64 and ARM64, distributed as `.deb` and `.rpm`. Source: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/changelog

platforms.name: Amazon Bedrock — one dated entry that exposed a months-old gap
details: **`bedrock-mantle` endpoint / Project Mantle.** The Aug 11 doc-history entry (IAM principal cost allocation extended to `bedrock-mantle`) is billing plumbing, but the endpoint it names appears **nowhere in this monitor's history**. `bedrock-mantle.<region>.api.aws` is a second, parallel Bedrock inference surface powered by "Project Mantle", a new distributed inference engine. It serves the **OpenAI Responses API, the OpenAI Chat Completions API and the Anthropic Messages API**, with **built-in tool use and stateful conversation management**, and AWS **recommends it over `bedrock-runtime` for new applications**. platforms.name: Google Gemini Enterprise — four dated entries, Aug 10–13
details: **Skills (Aug 13).** Users can **create, upload and share skills** — reusable custom instructions for specialized tasks. Each skill is a **package containing a `SKILL.md` prompt file**, and a package **can also include scripts, files, or background context**. An administrator must enable the skills feature, and separately enable **skill sharing**, which can be configured to **require administrator review or to allow immediate sharing**. Sharing is per-user by email address. GA behind an allowlist. A programmatic **Skill Registry** exists on the Agent Platform side. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/skills

Write actions include **create branch, create or update file, push file, update pull request, merge pull request, fork repository, update issues, add comment to an issue, add comment to a pending review**. Data federation sends the search query **directly to the GitHub API at query time** and blends results with other sources rather than indexing into a data store. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/connectors/github

**12 new data stores in public preview, plus new write actions on four existing connectors (Aug 11).** New: Cisco Workspaces, Fibery, Gong, Guru, Hex, LegalZoom, Mercury, Miro, Ramp, Solve Intelligence, **Vanta**, Webex Meetings. New actions: Airtable record updates, Hex threads, Miro document creation, Smartsheet row additions. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/connectors/connect-third-party-data-source
*(Not reported: AlphaEvolve HPC solution, Gemini 3.7 Flash, Gemini Omni Flash, CSV user export, invoiced-billing overage management.)*

findings.title: Anthropic Compliance API now exposes transcripts of Cowork and Claude Code sessions running on employee laptops
findings.description: Three new endpoints — `GET /v1/compliance/apps/sessions/local`, `.../local/{session_id}`, and `.../local/{session_id}/messages` — return the full conversation of agent sessions that execute **on users' own machines**, for Claude Enterprise organizations. Transcripts carry user prompts, assistant text, and **`tool_use` and `tool_result` blocks, with MCP tool calls and most server tool calls normalized into those same shapes**, so an agent's actual tool invocations and their returned data are readable. `product_surface` distinguishes `cowork` from `claude_code`, `CLAUDE.md` project instructions appear as ordinary user content, and skill content appears when the client sends it. This is the richest AIDR ingestion surface Anthropic has published and it requires **no new credential** — it reuses the same Compliance Access Key and `read:compliance_user_data` scope Zenity may already hold, and no client-side deployment. Two things demand equal attention. First, **the documented blind spots are a coverage map in themselves**: Claude Code authenticated with a Console API key or routed through **Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud or Microsoft Foundry** is not captured, nor is Claude Code on the web, nor anything in organizations with **HIPAA readiness** or under **ZDR**, and under **CMEK** sessions list but their content is withheld — so an enterprise can believe it has full local-agent visibility while its Bedrock-routed developers are entirely invisible. Second, **what is deliberately omitted from every transcript matters for detection**: thinking blocks, the system prompt, and — most significantly — **tool definitions and MCP server configuration**, meaning a transcript shows that a tool was called but never what that tool was permitted to do or which MCP server backed it. AIDR should ingest local sessions as a first-class agent-activity stream keyed on `product_surface`, join `user.id` to identity, and treat the excluded populations as explicit gaps to close by other means; AISPM should discover whether HIPAA/ZDR/CMEK settings are suppressing capture, since each silently disables it

findings.title: Microsoft Foundry agents can now be published as callable A2A servers with discoverable agent cards
findings.description: Foundry has added **incoming A2A** — the ability to expose an agent **as** an Agent2Agent endpoint that other agents discover and call — updated two days before this scan and the freshest change in it. Every prompt agent supports it by default, and enabling it takes a single PATCH that sets `agent_card` and adds `a2a` to `protocol_configuration`; it is **not exposed in the Foundry portal at all**, so it can only be turned on via REST or SDK and will be invisible to anyone auditing through the UI. The agent then publishes cards at `…/protocols/a2a/agentCard/v1.0` and `…/agentCard/v0.3` advertising its description and a **`skills[]` capability list** to any authorized caller. The finding Zenity most needs is the **version-negotiation default**: Foundry serves **both v1.0 and v0.3 on the same base path**, and **when a caller specifies no version, it serves v0.3** — so the protocol actually spoken on an endpoint is chosen by the *caller*, not by the endpoint's configuration, and an inventory that records "A2A v1.0" from the configuration will be wrong for any client that doesn't negotiate. The authorization model is the second half: all A2A URLs require Entra ID (**anonymous agent-card access is explicitly unsupported**, which is a genuine control worth verifying rather than assuming), callers need only **Foundry Agent Consumer** on the hosting project, and they may authenticate either **on-behalf-of an end user** or **with a service identity** — the latter meaning an agent-to-agent call chain with no human in it and no user context to scope against. AISPM should discover which agents have `a2a` in their `protocol_configuration`, inventory each published `agent_card` and its `skills[]` as the agent's advertised attack surface, enumerate every principal holding Foundry Agent Consumer as a potential caller, and flag agents reachable by service identity. AIRT should treat a published agent card as a discovery primitive and test whether inbound A2A content is handled as trusted instruction

findings.title: Microsoft Foundry connector namespaces turn 1,000+ SaaS connectors into auto-provisioned managed MCP servers hosted on logic.azure.com
findings.description: Adding any connector from the Foundry Tools Catalog now causes Foundry to provision a **managed MCP server** on the customer's behalf. Every Foundry account has a **Connector Namespace** — a managed service hosting connector runtimes and MCP servers — with **each project mapped to its own environment** inside it, and the namespace owns server hosting, tool definitions, authentication, credential management and lifecycle. Three properties make this a first-order inventory problem. First, **scale and provenance**: over 1,000 connectors span four publisher tiers with explicitly different data-handling — Microsoft internal (SharePoint, Teams, Dynamics 365), Microsoft external (GitHub), verified third-party (Docusign, Databricks, Box), and **independent publishers at what Microsoft calls a "lower certification bar"** — so the publisher tier of each attached connector is a posture signal, and Microsoft's own page warns that auth keys and prompt content may be passed to third-party tools and that "MCP implementations are vulnerable to attacks, cascading failures, and loss of human oversight." Second, **the endpoint is not where you would look for it**: the connection's `target` is rewritten from a literal `https://placeholder` to a **`logic.azure.com/api/connectorGateways/<envId>/mcpServerConfigs/<name>/mcp`** URL, so the real MCP endpoint lives on Logic Apps infrastructure, not on the Foundry project endpoint, and the connection is identifiable by `metadata.type = gateway_connector` with `category: RemoteTool`. Third, **the portal's safety rail does not exist in code**: only *validated* connectors surface the managed-MCP experience in the portal, but the docs state plainly that via REST, SDK or `azd` **"there's no gating — you can use any connector in the catalog."** Add that each end user must complete a **per-user OAuth consent**, so the effective reach of a tool is the union of every consenting user's permissions in the target SaaS. AISPM should enumerate project connections of type `gateway_connector`, resolve each to its connector, publisher tier and **registered operation list** (`mcpserverConfigProperties`), record the logic.azure.com gateway target as an inventory endpoint, flag connectors added through the code-first path that would not have passed portal validation, and treat write-capable operations as privileged

findings.title: OpenAI Computer History records everything a user does on macOS and feeds it to an ephemeral Codex agent
findings.description: ChatGPT's macOS desktop app has shipped an opt-in feature that converts **activity across all apps and websites** into memories and a timeline usable by ChatGPT and Codex. It records interaction events exposed through **macOS accessibility APIs** — clicks, typing, keyboard shortcuts, and app switching — which means keystrokes and UI interactions inside applications that have nothing to do with ChatGPT, including other security tools, terminals, password managers and internal business systems. The architecture is the finding: events are buffered on the Mac for up to 48 hours, and Computer History then **periodically starts an ephemeral Codex session with access to the raw interaction-event stream** to summarize it into memories; those temporary event files are **processed on OpenAI's servers** before the resulting **plain-text memory files are written back to local disk**, where they persist until deleted. So a general-purpose agent session is granted a feed of the user's entire desktop activity, and a durable plain-text derivative of it sits on the endpoint. It replaces the Chronicle preview and is a genuine rebuild — Chronicle captured screenshots, this does not, and it also excludes screen recordings, microphone and system audio — but the accessibility-event stream is arguably more sensitive than screenshots because it captures typed content directly. Governance hooks exist and should be inventoried: it is **off by default**, Pro users may self-enable, and **Business and Enterprise workspaces require an administrator to grant access before any member can turn it on**; users choose which apps and websites contribute and can pause collection from the menu bar; it is unavailable in the EEA, Switzerland and the UK. ENDPOINT should detect the ChatGPT macOS app's Computer History state per device, inventory the local memory files as a sensitive on-disk artifact, and alert when it is enabled on endpoints with access to regulated systems; AISPM should track the workspace-level admin grant as a tenant control; AIRT should consider whether content typed in one application can shape agent behaviour in another through the resulting memories

findings.title: OpenAI Daybreak Red grants access to GPT-5.6-Cyber, a model that answers 95% of exploit-development prompts
findings.description: OpenAI has added two tiers to its Daybreak "Trusted Access for Cyber" program. **Daybreak Blue** covers approved defensive workflows — secure code review, vulnerability triage, detection engineering, incident response, malware analysis, patch validation — on GPT-5.6 Sol with system-level safeguards. **Daybreak Red** goes further, covering advanced defensive **and offensive** cyber tasks with access to the purpose-trained **GPT-5.5-Cyber and GPT-5.6-Cyber** models for vulnerability research, exploit validation and security testing. The number that matters for Zenity is OpenAI's own published evaluation: **GPT-5.6-Cyber handled 95% of advanced cybersecurity prompts** spanning exploit-chain development, authentication bypass and privilege escalation, **while GPT-5.6 Sol with default protections answered 1.5%**. That is an explicit, vendor-documented ~63x differential in offensive capability gated only by program membership, and it changes the threat model in both directions. Defensively, a tenant where some identity holds Daybreak Red access has a materially different risk profile from one that does not, and that entitlement is a posture attribute Zenity should be able to discover and attest — including which users or service accounts hold it and whether their use is logged. Offensively, this is directly relevant to AIRT's own mandate: the capability differential defines a realistic upper bound for what an attacker with a compromised Red-tier credential could do against a customer's agents and infrastructure, and it makes the Daybreak entitlement itself a high-value credential worth protecting like any other. AIRT should incorporate the Blue/Red capability distinction into red-team scenario design and use the published differential to calibrate assumed adversary capability; AISPM should inventory Daybreak tier membership as a privileged entitlement on the OpenAI organization alongside admin roles

findings.title: Amazon Bedrock has a second inference endpoint — `bedrock-mantle` — serving OpenAI and Anthropic APIs with stateful conversations, and AWS now recommends it over `bedrock-runtime`
findings.description: `bedrock-mantle.<region>.api.aws`, powered by "Project Mantle", is a distributed inference engine running in parallel to `bedrock-runtime` and serving three API shapes Zenity's Bedrock coverage was not built for: the **OpenAI Responses API**, the **OpenAI Chat Completions API**, and the **Anthropic Messages API**. It adds **built-in tool use and stateful conversation management**, and AWS's stated migration pitch is that an existing OpenAI SDK codebase moves onto Bedrock by changing only the base URL and API key. AWS **recommends bedrock-mantle for new applications**, which means new Bedrock workloads will default onto it. This is a coverage gap rather than a fresh launch — it surfaced only because an August 11 cost-allocation note named it, but PrivateLink support for these endpoints landed in February 2026 and dedicated CloudWatch metrics and a redesigned console in June 2026, so the surface has been building for roughly six months while every scan looked at `bedrock-runtime` and the Agents APIs. Three consequences follow. Detection keyed on `bedrock-runtime` API shapes will **silently miss all mantle traffic**, and because the request/response formats are OpenAI's and Anthropic's rather than AWS's, parsing differs too. **Stateful conversation management** means conversation state now lives server-side in Bedrock, a data store that did not previously exist in this service and that Zenity does not inventory. And **built-in tool use** means tool invocation happens inside the endpoint, so the tool-call surface is not visible in the customer's own orchestration code. AISPM should add the mantle endpoint to Bedrock discovery, inventory IAM principals and PrivateLink endpoints reaching it, and reconcile mantle usage against known agent inventory; AIDR should add parsers for the OpenAI Responses, Chat Completions and Anthropic Messages shapes on this endpoint and treat its stateful conversations as a retained data location

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise Skills are shareable packages that can carry scripts and files, not just instructions
findings.description: Gemini Enterprise now lets users **create, upload and share skills**. The critical detail is the packaging model: each skill is a **package containing a `SKILL.md` prompt file**, and the package **can also include scripts, files, or background context** the assistant uses to complete the task. That makes a skill a distributable artifact that carries executable and data content between users, not merely a saved prompt — and it is a new inventory entity type with an owner, a body, attachments and a sharing graph. The sharing model is the governance surface: an administrator must enable the skills feature, and must **separately enable skill sharing**, which can be configured either to **require administrator review** or to **allow immediate sharing** — so whether a user-authored package containing scripts can propagate across the organization unreviewed is a single tenant toggle. Sharing itself is per-user by email address, producing exactly the kind of informal distribution graph that outruns governance. A programmatic **Skill Registry** exists on the Agent Platform side, giving Zenity an API path to enumerate them. AISPM should discover skills as an entity type with owner, contents and share list, record whether the tenant requires administrator review before sharing (and flag tenants that do not), inspect skill packages for scripts and embedded credentials, and treat a widely-shared skill as a high-blast-radius object. AIRT should treat skill content as an injection vector, since a shared skill's `SKILL.md` becomes instruction text in every recipient's agent context

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise GitHub connector reaches GA with write access to source control — merge pull requests, push files, create branches
findings.description: The GitHub connector is now generally available with **data federation**, and its action set is the finding: **create branch, create or update file, push file, update pull request, merge pull request, fork repository, update issues, add comment to an issue, add comment to a pending review**. An agent with this connector attached can therefore **modify source code and merge changes into repositories** — one of the highest-consequence write paths an enterprise agent can hold, since merged code reaches CI/CD and production. This is materially different from the read-only search connectors that make up most of the catalog and should not be inventoried in the same class. The federation mechanism adds a second consideration: rather than indexing content into a data store, Gemini Enterprise **sends the search query directly to the GitHub API at query time** and blends the results, which means access is evaluated live against the connecting credential and there is no indexed copy to inspect — so the connector's effective read scope is exactly whatever its GitHub credential can see, at the moment of query, and cannot be determined from a data-store inventory. AISPM should discover GitHub connector instances, resolve the authenticating GitHub identity and its repository scopes, enumerate which of the write actions are enabled on each agent, and flag any agent holding `merge pull request` or `push file` as a code-integrity risk requiring branch-protection compensating controls. AIRT should test whether prompt injection reaching such an agent can drive a merge or a file push

findings.title: Microsoft Foundry is relocating prompts, tool definitions, tool arguments and tool results into a separate protected trace table by September 30, 2026
findings.description: Foundry now classifies seven OpenTelemetry gen-AI attributes as sensitive content — `gen_ai.input.messages`, `gen_ai.output.messages`, `gen_ai.system_instructions`, **`gen_ai.tool.definitions`**, **`gen_ai.tool.call.arguments`**, **`gen_ai.tool.call.result`**, and `gen_ai.evaluation.explanation` — and routes them to a dedicated Log Analytics table, **`AppGenAIContent`**, which can be marked **Protected** so that only holders of the **Privileged Monitoring Data Reader** role can read it. This is both an operational deadline and a posture control. Operationally: **starting September 30, 2026, these attribute values stop being written to `AppDependencies`, `AppTraces` and `AppEvents` for newly ingested data** — the keys remain but the values are replaced with a short pointer to `AppGenAIContent`. **Any Zenity query, detection or ingestion path reading Foundry agent prompts, tool calls or tool results from those three tables will silently return pointers instead of content after that date**, which is a hard-dated breakage rather than a gradual drift, and the opt-out flag that defers it is itself discontinued on September 30, 2027. As posture: whether a customer has set `AppGenAIContent` to Protected, and who holds Privileged Monitoring Data Reader on it, determines who in the organization can read every prompt, system instruction and tool result their agents have produced — an unprotected table means standard Log Analytics readers can read all of it, and an over-broad grant of the privileged role is a serious exposure. AIDR should migrate Foundry trace ingestion to `AppGenAIContent` ahead of the deadline and ensure its identity holds the privileged role where the table is protected; AISPM should discover the table's protection level per workspace, inventory Privileged Monitoring Data Reader assignments as privileged access to agent conversation content, and flag workspaces where agent traces remain readable by standard roles

findings.title: ChatGPT desktop imports agent configuration — settings, skills, plugins and projects — from Claude Code, Claude Cowork and Cursor, with continuous sync
findings.description: The ChatGPT desktop app can now import **instructions, settings, skills, plugins, projects and recent work** from **Claude Code, Claude Cowork and Cursor**, and can be set to keep imported work **automatically in sync with the original agent**; Codex CLI offers the same via `/import` for Claude Code and Cursor. This matters to ENDPOINT coverage because it breaks the assumption that each local agent's configuration is independently governed. A skill, plugin or instruction set that was reviewed and approved in one tool now propagates into another vendor's agent — and with automatic updates on, it keeps propagating, so a change made in Cursor can land in ChatGPT without any further user action. Practically: a policy that governs Claude Code's plugins does not govern the copies now running under ChatGPT, and configuration drift between the two is invisible unless both are inventoried and compared. It also creates a lateral path for a malicious or compromised skill to spread across the endpoint's agent estate from a single point of entry. ENDPOINT should inventory local agent configurations per tool rather than per machine, detect whether import and automatic updates are enabled in the ChatGPT desktop app, and treat a skill or plugin present in two agents as one object with two enforcement points — reconciling them so an approval in one tool is not silently inherited by another

findings.title: Microsoft Foundry Canvas builds and deploys production Foundry agents from inside the GitHub Copilot App
findings.description: Foundry Canvas is a **GitHub Copilot App extension** that opens a side panel to design, configure, test and deploy Foundry **hosted agents** without leaving the editor. It signs the developer in to Azure, enumerates their subscriptions and Foundry projects, and browses the project's deployed models, **toolboxes, tools, skills and guardrails**, letting them be attached to a new agent; each choice becomes a prompt for Copilot, which writes the agent code. **Inspect Locally** runs the agent in an embedded **Agent Inspector**, and **Deploy to Foundry** publishes it — both by executing underlying `azd` commands. The coverage point is that a developer's IDE is now a **provisioning path into the customer's cloud agent estate**: agents can be created, wired to real tools and guardrails, and deployed to Foundry from a local editor extension, so agent creation events will originate from developer workstations rather than the portal or a CI pipeline, and the guardrail selection for a production agent is made in an editor side panel. The extension is installed from the Copilot App's plugin marketplace by searching `microsoft-foundry`, which is itself a supply-chain consideration for an extension holding Azure credentials. ENDPOINT should detect Foundry Canvas installation on developer endpoints and treat it as an agent-provisioning tool; AISPM should correlate Foundry agent-creation events back to the identity and workstation that ran `azd`, and flag agents deployed this way whose guardrail configuration diverges from policy

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise adds 12 data-source connectors and turns four read-only connectors into write-capable ones
findings.description: Twelve new data stores entered public preview — **Cisco Workspaces, Fibery, Gong, Guru, Hex, LegalZoom, Mercury, Miro, Ramp, Solve Intelligence, Vanta and Webex Meetings** — each extending the agent's reach into a new third-party system with natural-language search and read operations. Several carry unusually sensitive content for an agent to reach: **Gong** holds recorded sales conversations, **Mercury** and **Ramp** are financial systems, **LegalZoom** and **Solve Intelligence** hold legal and IP material, and **Vanta** holds the organization's own compliance and security posture data — an agent that can read Vanta can read the customer's control evidence and gaps. Separately, four existing connectors gained **write** actions: Airtable record updates, Hex threads, Miro document creation and Smartsheet row additions — meaning connectors previously inventoried as read-only now mutate third-party state, and any classification Zenity recorded for them is stale. AISPM should add the twelve connectors to its Gemini Enterprise inventory with data-sensitivity classification, re-evaluate the four changed connectors' read/write classification rather than trusting cached values, resolve the authenticating identity and scope for each connector instance, and flag agents holding write actions into financial or compliance systems

findings.title: ServiceNow AI Control Tower adds an agent map spanning models, MCP servers and cross-cloud providers, plus AI asset deduplication
findings.description: The Australia Patch 4 release of AI Control Tower adds an **agent map visualization** displaying **models, MCP servers, providers and workflows** across the enterprise, and a **deduplication** capability that identifies redundant AI assets for consolidation. Both are directly comparable to AISPM's own output, and both were absent from the prior scan's read of this page. The agent map matters because it explicitly includes **MCP servers** as first-class mapped entities alongside models and workflows — ServiceNow is building the same topology graph Zenity produces, sourced from its Service Graph connectors rather than from direct platform integration, which means for customers running both there will be two topology graphs of the same estate with different fidelity and different blind spots. Deduplication is the more actionable of the two: it presumes ServiceNow can tell when two discovered assets are the same underlying agent or model, which is precisely the reconciliation problem Zenity faces when correlating its own inventory against a customer's CMDB. AISPM should treat the ServiceNow agent map as a comparison inventory to reconcile against — divergence in either direction is a reportable finding — and should ingest deduplication decisions rather than recomputing them, so Zenity and ServiceNow do not disagree about how many agents a customer has

findings.title: ServiceNow AI Service Graph Connectors gain versioned per-vendor capabilities, including a Databricks connector that imports agents and an Anthropic connector that tracks per-user cost
findings.description: The connector set behind AI Control Tower now has stated versions and differentiated capabilities: **Anthropic v2.0.7** discovers models and tracks **per-user costs**, **GCP Vertex AI v1.2.4** has been renamed **"AI Connector for Google"**, **Microsoft** uses a unified Azure ML configuration with **certificate-based authentication**, **Amazon** consolidates to a single credential page with **automatic key rotation**, and **Databricks discovers *and imports* AI agents**. Two details raise this above routine connector churn. The Databricks connector **imports** agents rather than merely discovering them, meaning ServiceNow becomes an authoritative record for agents originating in Databricks — a system Zenity should know is in the customer's AI estate even where it has no direct integration. And the Anthropic connector tracking **per-user cost** means ServiceNow now holds per-individual usage data for a third-party AI platform, which is both a useful signal and a privacy-relevant data flow. The renaming of the Vertex connector is a small but real detection hazard: any Zenity logic matching that connector by name will miss it. Underneath all of them sits the concern flagged previously — each connector is a **standing set of cross-cloud credentials held inside the ServiceNow instance**, now with per-vendor authentication mechanisms worth evaluating individually (certificate-based for Microsoft, rotating keys for Amazon). AISPM should inventory configured connectors by version and vendor, match on identifiers rather than display names, resolve the identity and scope each authenticates with in the target cloud, and use the connector set to infer which AI platforms a customer runs

findings.title: Microsoft Foundry Notification Center aggregates Defender security alerts and guardrail policy violations into a portal-only feed
findings.description: Foundry has added a **Notification Center** that centralizes alerts for agents, models and projects into a single in-app feed, replacing what previously required manually configured Azure Monitor alerts across siloed systems. It covers four categories, two of which are security-relevant: **security alerts from Microsoft Defender for Cloud** — high-severity issues including malicious activity and **content safety violations** flagged against agents or their underlying infrastructure, surfaced through Azure's security alert APIs — and **policy and compliance notifications** from Azure Policy and **Foundry's built-in guardrails**, including ML governance policy violations. The rest are run completion and failure events for evaluations and training jobs. Zenity should care for two reasons. It is a **signal source**: guardrail violations and Defender detections against Foundry agents are exactly the events AIDR produces, so they should be correlated rather than duplicated, and the notification feed indicates what the platform itself already caught. And it is a **posture gap in its own right**: delivery is currently **portal-only in-app**, with no email or webhook channel documented, which means these security and compliance alerts are seen only by someone who logs into the Foundry portal and clicks the bell — high-severity Defender alerts about agents have no push path to a SOC. AISPM should record which Foundry projects have Defender for Cloud coverage and guardrail policies configured, and flag the absence of any external delivery channel for these alerts as an operational finding; AIDR should treat the alert categories as a correlation source

findings.title: Claude API responses now identify their originating workspace via the `anthropic-workspace-id` header
findings.description: Every Claude API response now carries an `anthropic-workspace-id` header holding the `wrkspc_`-prefixed ID of the workspace that the request's API key or access token resolved to, including the organization's Default Workspace. This is a small addition with real attribution value: workspaces are Anthropic's unit of spend, rate-limit and access segmentation, and until now the workspace behind a given key had to be looked up out-of-band or inferred. With the header, **every API response self-identifies its governance boundary**, which lets Zenity attribute observed traffic to a workspace directly from the response rather than maintaining a key-to-workspace mapping that drifts as keys are rotated or reassigned. The Default Workspace case is the useful signal: traffic resolving to the Default Workspace indicates a key that was never deliberately scoped to a purpose-built workspace, which is a reasonable posture finding on its own for organizations that have adopted workspace segmentation. AISPM should capture the header where it observes Claude API traffic, use it to build and continuously verify the key-to-workspace mapping, and flag production workloads resolving to the Default Workspace

findings.title: ChatGPT desktop app is now available on Linux, extending the endpoint agent surface to a third OS
findings.description: The ChatGPT desktop application entered preview for **Ubuntu, Debian and Fedora** on **x64 and ARM64**, distributed as `.deb` and `.rpm` packages. This is a straightforward but real expansion of ENDPOINT's scope: the same desktop agent Zenity tracks on macOS and Windows now runs on developer and server-adjacent Linux workstations, where endpoint agent tooling is typically thinnest and where package installation via `.deb`/`.rpm` may bypass the managed software channels used on the other two platforms. Detection logic, installation-path assumptions and configuration-file locations built for macOS and Windows will not carry over. Note the contrast with the Computer History finding above: that feature is macOS-only, so the Linux client has a different capability profile, and ENDPOINT should model per-OS feature availability rather than treating "ChatGPT desktop" as one uniform surface. ENDPOINT should add Linux package detection for the ChatGPT desktop app, establish its configuration and data paths, and extend existing macOS/Windows policy checks to the new platform

platforms.name: Microsoft Foundry / Microsoft 365 — backlog recovery (agent identity & control plane)
details: **Microsoft Agent 365 — generally available since May 1, 2026** for the Commercial segment, licensed per user (Microsoft E5 recommended; at least one qualifying Agent 365 / M365 Copilot license required). Microsoft's enterprise **control plane for AI agents**, built on Entra Agent ID, organised as observe / govern / secure. Five capabilities: **Registry** (tenant-wide inventory of Foundry agents, Copilot Studio agents, admin-registered agents and **shadow agents discovered in the tenant**, with ownership tracking for attestation; plus Registry sync and **Agent Map**), **Access control** (Entra RBAC + ABAC and risk-based Conditional Access), **Visualization** (connections between agents, people and data; real-time behaviour monitoring), **Interoperability** (access to M365 apps and org data; can connect to Work IQ), and **Security** (Microsoft Defender threat detection, Microsoft Purview information protection, DLP and compliance controls on agent activity). A set of **pre-integrated ecosystem partner agents** is deployable directly from the Microsoft 365 admin center. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-agent-365/overview

**Agent Registry in the Microsoft 365 admin center** — the concrete inventory. Four agent types (Microsoft, external partner-built, published by your org, shared by creator); tenant-wide counters for **Total agents**, **Agents without owners** and **Unmanaged agents** ("created or managed outside of Agent 365, without its risk protection and observability"); filters on status, publisher type, **channel** (Copilot, Teams, Outlook, M365 apps, SharePoint), **platform**, and **data source** (embedded knowledge, fine-tuned models). A **Risks** column aggregates high-severity risk across Entra, Defender and Purview, with a documented ten-type taxonomy: **Shadow agent** (Critical — no registry entry, no owner, or no Entra Agent ID), **No owner assigned** (Critical), **Excessive permissions** (Critical — access rights exceed declared function), **Security misconfiguration** (High), **Prompt injection** (High — AI Prompt Shield flags/blocks at runtime), **Sensitive data access** (High — labeled data accessed without a matching DLP exception), **Conditional access violation** (High), **Pending approval** (Medium), **Operational exceptions** (Medium), **Compliance/retention gap** (Medium). Export to Excel carries **over 30 attributes per agent**. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/admin/manage/agent-registry

**Package Management API — programmatic agent inventory and control (partly preview)** — a "package" represents an agent in the organization catalog. `GET /copilot/admin/catalog/packages` lists every agent in the organisation, filterable by **host** (Copilot, Outlook, Teams), **platform** (Copilot Studio, M365 Copilot Agent Builder), last-updated time, and **element types contained in the package** (bots, declarative agents and more); `GET /copilot/admin/catalog/packages/{id}` returns detailed metadata including `declarativeAgent` / `customEngineAgent` element objects. Four **write** operations are in preview: `PATCH .../{id}` (update metadata), `POST .../{id}/block`, `POST .../{id}/unblock`, and `POST .../{id}/reassign` (reassign package ownership). Resources: `copilotPackage`, `copilotPackageDetail`. **Access requires a Microsoft Agent 365 license**; the registry docs state the API works with the **AI Administrator** role. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365-copilot/extensibility/api/admin-settings/package/overview

**Autopilot agents (preview) and autopilot publishing from Foundry** — a new agent *category*. Each autopilot receives its own **Entra Agent ID user account with a productivity license, email, calendar, OneDrive and Teams presence**, and is designed for shared spaces such as Teams group chats rather than 1:1 chat. The interaction model shifts from prompt→response to **goal → ongoing execution → checkpoints → collaboration**: it surfaces progress, requests approvals and escalates to a human natively inside Teams and M365. A Foundry **Hosted** agent is published as an autopilot; the publish submits a request that creates an **agent blueprint** in the Microsoft 365 admin center, an **AI Administrator or Global Administrator** approves it, and it then appears in the Agent 365 registry and can be instantiated in Teams. Provisioning footprint includes an **Azure Bot Service** resource (Foundry-scoped roles do not carry `Microsoft.BotService/*`), Container Registry, and Application Insights + Log Analytics. Enablement requires a M365 Copilot license **plus enrollment in the Frontier preview program**, and a global admin accepting terms. Reference implementation is the **Workstream Manager** sample. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/agent-365

**Foundry ↔ Agent 365 data flow, logging and residency** — published Foundry agents sync automatically into the Agent 365 registry. Per-Foundry-resource logging is governed by the **`agent365Config` resource provider configuration**, and no data flows without both a valid license and accepted terms even when the ARM property is enabled. Critically, **Foundry follows the Azure region of the resource for data residency while Agent 365 follows the Entra tenant's storage location** — activity data crossing from Foundry into Agent 365 moves between two different residency models. Individual Foundry resources can be opted out. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/agent-365-integration

**New Foundry agent object model (replaces Agent Applications)** — collapses the **Agent Application** and **Deployment** control-plane objects into the **Agent** object. New agent properties: `agent_endpoint` (stable endpoint), `protocol_configuration`, `authorization_schemes`, `version_selector`, `blueprint`, `instance_identity`, and **`agent_card`** (surfaces the agent's details and capabilities to consumers and to **A2A**). Every newly created agent now receives a unique **Entra Agent Blueprint and Entra Agent Identity by default, at creation** — creating an agent is the only step needed to get a stable endpoint and a unique identity, and "publishing" now means only distribution to M365/Teams. Legacy agents are identified by a **null `instance_identity` / `agent.identity`**, share the project identity, and cannot be published via the stable endpoint; there is **no in-place upgrade** — you must recreate the agent. Endpoint format changed from `/applications/{app}/protocols/openai` to `/agents/{agent}/endpoint/protocols/openai/responses`. Agent Application deprecation is **planned**, end of support TBD. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/migrate-agent-applications

platforms.name: ServiceNow — Australia release AI stack (held item resolved + new application)
details: **MCP Server Console — new application in the Australia release.** Plugin **Model Context Protocol Server (`sn_mcp_server`)**, version 1.3. Enables governed access to ServiceNow instance functionality for AI applications via MCP. Unified MCP server creation with **embedded OAuth client registration**; **tool creation from Subflows, Actions, REST APIs, Knowledge Graphs and Now Assist skills**; a preconfigured **Quickstart Server** for incident and case record operations; administrator annotation configuration across all tool types; **third-party IDP** integration for user authentication and OAuth 2.0 client connectivity; and **MCP app creation** for interactive tool interfaces with client-side display per the MCP spec. Integrates with AI Control Tower for observability and with Machine Identity Console for OAuth inbound integrations. Requires a Now Assist deployment (Foundation, Advanced or Prime tier). Vendor and partner coverage adds that the **Action Fabric MCP Server is GA in every Now Assist and AI Native SKU**, that any MCP-compatible agent can discover and execute governed ServiceNow actions, and that **Anthropic Claude integration is live** (Claude can trigger workflows, catalog actions and approvals through the MCP Server). Source: https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/release-notes/mcp-server-console-rn.html

**AI Control Tower — Australia release, redesigned. HELD ITEM RESOLVED.** Available in the Australia release through the ServiceNow Store (request to install), described as enhanced and updated in Australia. New capabilities: an **Activity Center** unifying governance tasks, security items and AI recommendations; **Quality & Safety monitoring** with automated scoring, trend analysis and configurable metrics across portfolios; **agent lifecycle management that can deactivate and reinstate agents in AWS Bedrock, GCP Vertex AI and ServiceNow**; risk and compliance integration surfacing regulatory classifications on asset records; **customizable security scoring with weighted LLM guardrail categories**; threat-detection metrics for **system prompt leakage, sensitive data disclosure and injection attacks**; compliance scoring against configured regulatory frameworks; and **risk heat mapping** of inherent vs residual risk. MCP-side: **global MCP clients** usable across multiple servers, **MCP Catalog** integration for server selection, monitoring charts for MCP server access, and agent publishing through an **"External Registry" integration with Microsoft**. **AI Gateway is deprecated in the Australia release and no longer supported**, though legacy MCP client-server interactions stay visible through it. Source: https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/release-notes/ai-control-tower-rn.html

**AI Service Graph Connectors** — discovery of AI assets from **AWS** (with automatic key rotation and multi-account support), **Microsoft** (Azure ML and Copilot, certificate-based authentication), **GCP Vertex AI**, **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **Databricks** and others, feeding the Control Tower inventory. Source: https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/release-notes/ai-control-tower-rn.html

*(Held below bar: **Machine Identity Console**, which manages machine identities and OAuth inbound integrations and is the identity substrate the MCP Server Console depends on — it is genuinely outside Zenity's coverage, but it was introduced in the **Zurich** release and only enhanced in Australia, so it is not a new addition. AI Gateway's deprecation is a deprecation.)*

findings.title: Microsoft Agent 365 — a GA, tenant-wide agent control plane with its own shadow-agent discovery
findings.description: Microsoft Agent 365 has been generally available since **May 1, 2026** and this monitor has never reported it. It is Microsoft's enterprise control plane for AI agents, built on Entra Agent ID, and it maintains a **tenant-wide registry of every agent in the organisation regardless of where it was built** — Foundry agents, Copilot Studio agents, admin-registered agents, pre-integrated third-party partner agents deployable straight from the M365 admin center, and **shadow agents it discovers in the tenant itself**. It layers on Entra RBAC/ABAC and risk-based Conditional Access, Purview information protection and DLP, and Defender threat detection over agent activity. Two things make this urgent rather than merely interesting. First, it is a **new inventory surface Zenity must discover and reconcile**: an agent that exists in the Agent 365 registry but not in Zenity's inventory is a coverage gap, and the reverse is a governance gap Zenity can report on. Second, it **overlaps AISPM's own function** — a customer with Agent 365 enabled already has a partial agent inventory with ownership and risk signals, so Zenity needs to know what Agent 365 does and does not see (notably: it is licence-gated, requires a global admin to accept terms, and its own docs concede that "unmanaged agents" created outside it lack its risk protection and observability). AISPM should discover whether Agent 365 is enabled per tenant, ingest its registry as a comparison inventory, and treat divergence between the two inventories as a finding in its own right

findings.title: Microsoft 365 Agent Registry — a formal agent risk taxonomy and inventory schema Zenity should reconcile against
findings.description: The Agent 365 registry in the Microsoft 365 admin center exposes a concrete, documented inventory model that maps almost one-to-one onto AISPM's own concerns, and Zenity is not currently reading it. It classifies agents into four publisher types, filters them by **channel** (Copilot, Teams, Outlook, M365 apps, SharePoint), **platform**, and **data source** (embedded knowledge files uploaded by the maker, and **fine-tuned models** produced by M365 Copilot Tuning), and exports **over 30 attributes per agent**. It carries tenant-level counters for **agents without owners** and **unmanaged agents**, and a **Risks** column aggregating high-severity risk from Entra, Defender and Purview against a ten-type taxonomy that includes **Shadow agent** (Critical — defined as having no registry entry, no owner, or no Entra Agent ID), **Excessive permissions** (Critical — access rights exceeding declared function, i.e. a least-privilege violation), **Prompt injection** (High — flagged by AI Prompt Shield at runtime), **Sensitive data access** (High — labeled data accessed without a matching DLP exception), and **Conditional access violation** (High). This is both an opportunity and a competitive baseline: these are the exact toxic combinations AISPM reports, now computed natively by the platform. AISPM should ingest the registry's attributes as inventory enrichment (especially channel, platform, embedded-knowledge and fine-tuned-model flags, and owner), map Microsoft's risk types onto Zenity's violation rules so findings can be deduplicated rather than duplicated, and specifically target the gaps — Microsoft surfaces only **high**-severity risks in this column, with up to an hour of lag, and its shadow-agent definition is Entra-registration-based, so agents with a valid Entra Agent ID but no real ownership or oversight will not trip it

findings.title: Microsoft 365 Package Management API — a tenant-wide agent inventory endpoint that also blocks agents and reassigns their ownership
findings.description: Microsoft has put the Agent 365 agent catalog behind a Graph-style admin API where a "package" is an agent. `GET /copilot/admin/catalog/packages` returns every agent in the organisation — filterable by **host** (Copilot, Outlook, Teams), **platform** (Copilot Studio, M365 Copilot Agent Builder), last-updated time, and the **element types inside the package** (bots, declarative agents and more) — and `GET /copilot/admin/catalog/packages/{id}` returns per-agent metadata including the `declarativeAgent` and `customEngineAgent` element objects. This is the single most useful integration point in this report: it is how Zenity can enumerate Microsoft-side agents across every host surface in one call instead of inferring them per product, with element-level detail that reveals what an agent actually contains. It needs a posture rule as well as an integration, because the API is **not read-only**: `PATCH /{id}`, `POST /{id}/block`, `POST /{id}/unblock` and `POST /{id}/reassign` (reassign ownership to a different user) are all available in preview. Combined with the registry docs' statement that the API works with the **AI Administrator** role, that means an AI Administrator can enumerate the entire agent estate *and* disable agents or transfer their ownership — a privileged, low-friction control path that deserves both access review and activity monitoring. AISPM should adopt the list/detail endpoints as a discovery source for the Microsoft estate, inventory AI Administrator assignments as a privileged role, and treat block/unblock/reassign calls as auditable agent-lifecycle events. Note the whole API requires a **Microsoft Agent 365 license**, so it is unavailable in unlicensed tenants — Zenity's Microsoft discovery cannot depend on it alone

findings.title: Microsoft Foundry autopilot agents — agents provisioned as licensed Entra users with a mailbox, calendar, OneDrive and Teams presence
findings.description: Foundry Hosted agents can now be published as **autopilots** into Agent 365, and an autopilot is not a bot behind an endpoint — it is an **Entra Agent ID user account carrying a productivity licence, an email address, a calendar, OneDrive storage and a Teams presence**, living inside shared spaces like group chats. Its interaction model is explicitly **goal → ongoing execution → checkpoints → collaboration**: it is assigned an objective, works continuously, requests approvals and escalates to humans on its own initiative. This collapses the distinction Zenity's inventory relies on between "identities" and "agents": an autopilot must be modelled simultaneously as an agent (with a Foundry-side tool, memory and toolbox configuration) and as a **mailbox-bearing directory principal** that can receive mail, hold meetings and store files — a data-exfiltration and phishing surface no agent-shaped entity previously had. Three concrete inventory items follow: the **Entra Agent ID user account and its licence**, the **agent blueprint** created in the Microsoft 365 admin center and the identity of the AI/Global Administrator who approved it, and the **Azure Bot Service resource** in the publish path (notable because Foundry-scoped roles deliberately exclude `Microsoft.BotService/*`, so publishing requires a separate, broader Owner/Contributor grant at resource-group scope). AISPM should discover autopilots as a distinct entity type, join the Foundry-side capability graph to the M365-side user account, flag autopilots whose mailbox or OneDrive is reachable from outside the tenant, and treat the approval record as the authorisation artifact to audit. AIRT should test whether content delivered to an autopilot's mailbox or a Teams group chat is treated as trusted instruction

findings.title: Microsoft Foundry replaced its agent object model — every agent now gets a unique Entra identity and an A2A-discoverable agent card at creation
findings.description: Foundry has **collapsed the Agent Application and Deployment control-plane objects into the Agent object itself**, and the consequences reach directly into how agents must be inventoried. Every newly created agent now receives a **unique Entra Agent Blueprint and Entra Agent Identity by default, at creation** — previously identity was only minted at publish and unpublished agents shared one project identity. Agents gained `agent_endpoint` (a stable endpoint that exists from creation, with no publish step), `authorization_schemes`, `protocol_configuration`, `version_selector`, `instance_identity`, and **`agent_card`**, which advertises the agent's details and capabilities to consumers **and to A2A** — meaning every agent is now potentially discoverable and callable by other agents by default. Zenity must handle the resulting **three-population problem**: new agents (non-null `instance_identity`, unique identity, all features), legacy agents (**null `instance_identity`**, sharing the project identity, backfilled with the new properties but unpublishable), and surviving Agent Applications as separate resources — and because Microsoft provides **no in-place upgrade**, customers will migrate by recreating agents, producing duplicate logical agents with different identities and endpoints during the transition. AISPM should key Foundry agent discovery on `instance_identity` to segment these populations, inventory `agent_card` contents as the agent's advertised capability set, treat a null identity as a posture finding (shared-identity blast radius), and detect the old and new endpoint URL forms as the same logical agent

findings.title: Microsoft Foundry Agent Applications are ARM resources that Microsoft states are NOT in the Entra agent registry
findings.description: Published Foundry agents exist as first-class Azure resources — `Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/projects/applications` with child `agentDeployments` — each wrapping an agent version with its own dedicated endpoint (`baseUrl`), its own `agentIdentityBlueprint` and `defaultInstanceIdentity`, an `authorizationPolicy`, and a `trafficRoutingPolicy`. The finding is Microsoft's own explicit statement that **"Foundry Agent Applications are not registered in the Microsoft Entra agent registry."** That is a documented blind spot at the centre of Microsoft's own agent governance story: an organisation relying on the Entra Agent ID registry or the Agent 365 registry for its agent inventory **will not see agents published this way**, even though each one is a live, independently addressable, internet-reachable endpoint running with its own identity. Zenity can close a gap the platform vendor has admitted to. AISPM should enumerate these ARM resources directly via Azure Resource Manager rather than relying on any Entra- or Agent-365-derived inventory, resolve each application's identity and deployment state, record `authorizationPolicy` (noting that **API-key auth is not supported**, so every caller is an Entra principal that can be resolved) and `trafficRoutingPolicy`, and flag applications that are enabled with a running deployment but absent from the tenant's agent registry

findings.title: Microsoft Foundry agent identity blueprints — class-level credentials that mint agent identities, and unattended app-only agent auth
findings.description: Foundry's identity model introduces two Entra object types Zenity should treat as first-class inventory. An **agent identity** is a special service principal representing one agent at runtime; an **agent identity blueprint** is the governing object for an entire *class* of agents, and it **holds the OAuth credentials — client secret, certificate, or federated credential — used to create and impersonate every agent identity beneath it**. A blueprint is therefore a high-value credential whose compromise implies control of a whole class of agents, and its credential type is a posture signal (Microsoft recommends federated/managed identity precisely to avoid stored secrets, but client secrets and certificates are supported and require manual rotation). Blueprints are also the correct enforcement point: Conditional Access, bulk disable and revocation all apply at blueprint level. Separately, agents authenticate in one of two modes, and the distinction is the finding: **attended** (on-behalf-of, so the agent can only reach what the user consented to) versus **unattended** (client-credentials/app-only, where **no human is involved and access is bounded only by the agent's own RBAC and Graph app permissions**). An unattended agent with broad role assignments is an autonomous, fully-privileged actor. AISPM should inventory blueprints and their credential types, map each agent identity to its blueprint, record which agents run unattended, resolve `agentIdentityId` role assignments across downstream resources to compute effective reach, and flag the documented failure mode that **permissions do not transfer when an agent is published** — which in practice pushes operators toward over-granting on the new identity

findings.title: ServiceNow MCP Server Console — a ServiceNow instance becomes a governed MCP server exposing workflows as agent tools
findings.description: The Australia release adds an entirely new application, **MCP Server Console** (plugin `sn_mcp_server`, v1.3), that turns a ServiceNow instance into an MCP server any MCP-compatible AI agent can call. Its significance is what becomes a *tool*: administrators can expose **Subflows, Actions, REST APIs, Knowledge Graphs and Now Assist skills** as MCP tools, with a preconfigured Quickstart Server for incident and case record operations. That means arbitrary ServiceNow automation — approvals, catalog actions, record mutation, workflow execution — is now reachable by external agents, and vendor coverage confirms the **Action Fabric MCP Server is GA across every Now Assist and AI Native SKU** with **Anthropic Claude integration live**. Each MCP server is a new inventory entity with an endpoint, an **embedded OAuth client registration**, an authentication configuration that can delegate to a **third-party IDP**, and a tool list whose blast radius is defined by the underlying subflow or REST API rather than by anything visible on the MCP surface. **MCP apps** additionally allow interactive, client-side-rendered tool interfaces, which is a UI-injection surface. AISPM should discover MCP servers and their registered tools on ServiceNow instances, resolve each tool back to the subflow/action/API it wraps and the privileges that carries, record the OAuth client and IDP binding, and flag write-capable tools reachable by external agents. AIRT should treat these tools as a prompt-injection-to-privileged-action path, since a compromised agent conversation now maps directly onto ServiceNow workflow execution

findings.title: ServiceNow AI Control Tower (Australia) — cross-cloud agent governance that can deactivate agents in AWS Bedrock and GCP Vertex AI
findings.description: The long-held AI Control Tower question is resolved: it ships in the **Australia release** via the ServiceNow Store, substantially redesigned, and **AI Gateway is deprecated and no longer supported**. The new capability set is a third-party agent-governance surface that overlaps AISPM directly and, in one respect, exceeds it: **agent lifecycle management that can deactivate and reinstate agents in AWS Bedrock, GCP Vertex AI and ServiceNow** — a control-plane *action* on agents in other clouds, executed from ServiceNow. Alongside it: an **Activity Center** consolidating governance tasks and security items; **Quality & Safety monitoring** with automated scoring and configurable metrics; **customizable security scoring with weighted LLM guardrail categories** and threat-detection metrics for **system prompt leakage, sensitive data disclosure and injection attacks**; compliance scoring against regulatory frameworks with **risk heat mapping** of inherent vs residual risk; **global MCP clients** usable across multiple servers plus **MCP Catalog** integration and MCP server access monitoring; and agent publishing through an **"External Registry" integration with Microsoft**. Zenity needs this on two levels. As inventory: Control Tower is a new governance control plane whose enablement, connectors and scoring configuration are posture-relevant, and whose cross-cloud deactivation capability is a **privileged action on agents that must be audited** — whoever can deactivate a Bedrock agent from ServiceNow holds real power over another cloud's workloads. As positioning: its guardrail categories and threat metrics are the same detections AIDR produces, so findings should be correlated rather than duplicated. AISPM should discover AI Control Tower deployments, inventory their connected clouds and configured scoring weights, and treat cross-cloud lifecycle actions as high-value audit events

findings.title: ServiceNow AI Service Graph Connectors — third-party AI asset discovery across AWS, Microsoft, GCP, Anthropic, OpenAI and Databricks
findings.description: AI Control Tower now ships **AI Service Graph Connectors** that discover AI assets from **AWS** (with automatic key rotation and multi-account support), **Microsoft** (Azure ML and Copilot, using certificate-based authentication), **GCP Vertex AI**, **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **Databricks** and others, populating the ServiceNow CMDB with third-party AI inventory. Each connector is a new inventory entity, and each is also a **standing set of cross-cloud read credentials held inside ServiceNow** — a Microsoft certificate, AWS keys with rotation, GCP and vendor API credentials — which makes the ServiceNow instance a concentration point for access to every AI platform the customer runs. That is a credential-sprawl and lateral-movement concern that belongs in AISPM regardless of what the connectors discover. It is also the most direct inventory overlap with Zenity in this report: for customers running both, the same agents and models will be discovered twice by different mechanisms with different fidelity. AISPM should discover which AI Service Graph Connectors are configured, resolve the identity and scope each authenticates with in the target cloud, flag over-permissioned or non-rotating connector credentials, and use the connector set to predict which AI platforms a customer runs even where Zenity has no direct integration

findings.title: Microsoft Foundry RBAC roles renamed, plus new per-agent role assignment scope
findings.description: Foundry's built-in roles have been renamed — **Azure AI User / Owner / Account Owner / Project Manager** are now **Foundry User / Owner / Account Owner / Project Manager** — with role IDs and permissions unchanged, and Microsoft explicitly advises using role definition GUIDs instead of names because both sets of names are in circulation during rollout. Any Zenity discovery rule, policy or report that matches Foundry permissions on **role name** will silently miss renamed assignments and under-report privilege; this is a small change with a quiet failure mode, which is why it is worth a finding. Two associated details matter for least-privilege analysis: a **Foundry Agent Consumer** role now exists for principals that only invoke agents (so seeing Foundry User where Agent Consumer would suffice is an over-grant worth flagging), and roles can now be assigned at the scope of an **individual agent** (`.../projects/{project}/agents/{agent}`) — a new, finer scope Zenity's permission model should represent, with the caveat that Microsoft currently evaluates agent-scope assignments **only** for endpoint access and not for control-plane operations, so an agent-scoped assignment can look more restrictive than it behaves. AISPM should key Foundry role detection on role definition GUIDs, add the agent scope to its permission graph, and flag Foundry User grants where Foundry Agent Consumer would be sufficient

findings.title: Microsoft Agent 365 activity ingestion and the Foundry→Agent 365 data-residency crossing
findings.description: Enabling Agent 365 causes **agent activity data from Foundry to be ingested into the Agent 365 control plane**, where it powers the registry, analytics dashboards and security features — making Agent 365 a new, retained activity stream covering agents across the tenant and therefore an AIDR ingestion candidate. Two properties make it more than a feed. First, ingestion is governed per Foundry resource by the **`agent365Config` resource provider configuration**, and the whole pipeline is additionally gated on tenant licensing and a global administrator having accepted terms — so **an agent can be fully governed on paper while its activity is silently not being collected**, and the state of that per-resource config is a posture signal rather than a detail. Second, **Foundry and Agent 365 use different data-residency models**: Foundry follows the Azure region of the resource, Agent 365 follows the **Entra tenant's storage location**, so activity data crossing between them moves from region-scoped to tenant-scoped residency and may leave the geography the Foundry resource was deliberately placed in. Microsoft's mitigation is per-resource opt-out, which means residency compliance here is a per-resource setting nobody is likely to audit. AIDR should ingest Agent 365 activity as an agent-behaviour source; AISPM should record `agent365Config` state per Foundry resource, flag resources where governance is assumed but collection is disabled, and treat the residency crossing as a data-flow finding for regulated tenants

platforms.name: Claude Enterprise (Anthropic)
details: **Session budgets for Claude Managed Agents** — a hard cap on a session's spend, priced at public list rates. A session that reaches its budget pauses with the `budget_reached` stop reason instead of starting new model requests; changing or removing the budget resumes it. Deployments accept the same budget and apply it to every session they start. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/budgets

**Session advisor** — a session can be given an advisor: a model *at least as capable as the agent's own* that the session's primary thread consults mid-turn for strategic guidance. Configured as a `{"type": "advisor"}` entry in the agent's multiagent roster, naming the `model` to consult. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/multiagent-orchestration#give-the-session-an-advisor

**`inference_geo` — per-agent and per-session inference location control** — set inside the `model` object when creating a Managed Agents agent, or overridden for a single session, selecting the geo where model inference runs. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/data-residency

**Skills loaded from a GitHub repository** — when a Managed Agents session mounts a repository, any skills in its root `.claude/skills` directory are **discovered automatically at session start** and available to the agent for that session. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/skills#load-skills-from-a-github-repository

*(Held below bar: Dreams research preview adding Claude Opus 5 support, Aug 1. Anthropic News carries only the Aug 7 Fable 5 biology-safeguards post and an Aug 4 leadership appointment — no new product surface.)*

platforms.name: Google Gemini Enterprise
details: **Custom MCP server data stores — GA (August 7, 2026)** — organizations can connect their own Model Context Protocol server to Gemini Enterprise to reach private company data, custom internal tools and MCP-compliant third-party systems. The capability is **off by default** and gated behind administrator approval via an organization policy constraint (with a documented override path). Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/connectors/custom-mcp-server/set-up-custom-mcp-server
